name: Chloe Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a front-end loader on the ROM pad at the nickel mine. ROM means run-of-mine, it's the big stockpile where the trucks drop the ore before it goes to the crusher, and my job is to blend it and feed the crusher so it gets the right mix. It's a bit like baking, you can't just throw it all in. My grandad worked underground at this same mine, and my dad was a fitter here for 35 years, so it's in the family.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know exactly what I'm doing and nobody has to tell me. What wears me out is the shifts and the money. My husband Mark is a heavy diesel mechanic at the same mine, so we're both on rosters, and his mum helps a lot with Hannah, who's 14, and Luke, who's 11. We're both on the lower rates because the mine was sold three years ago and the new owners put everyone hired after a certain date on a lower scale. Sunday is church and lunch at Mark's mum's, and that's the one fixed thing in our week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every few years the city people come up with some new thing that's going to change the world, and the ore still has to be dug. I'd say it to Mark's mum over Sunday lunch, I don't go online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's what I'd hope for. I don't want to learn some new system at this stage, and I don't trust it. If things stay the same, we can get ahead a bit and maybe pay off the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. Keep doing my shifts, keep going to church, keep the kids' routine. Maybe try to put a bit aside after the car's paid off, but I'm not going to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. That's the word. Like the ground stays put under you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust it. What is it about AI that you don't trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's made by people who've never had dirt under their nails, telling the rest of us how to live. Hannah's teacher had them use it for an essay and it made up a quote from a book that doesn't exist. If it can't get that right, I don't want it near my crusher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the car money once it's paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put it toward Hannah's braces, probably, the dentist quoted $6,000. Or save it. We'd talk about it, Mark and me, and pray on it.

S0.say: She'd say she isn't surprised, since city people always promise world-changing things while the ore still has to be dug. She'd say it at Sunday lunch, not online.
S0.think: It's what she hopes for, since she doesn't want to learn a new system now and doesn't trust it. If things stay the same the family can get ahead and pay off the car.
S0.do: Carries on with shifts, church and the kids' routine. Plans to put the car payment toward braces or savings once the loan is paid off.
S0.feel: Settled, like the ground staying put.
S0.quote: It's made by people who've never had dirt under their nails, telling the rest of us how to live.
S0.fieldNote: Her distrust of AI is rooted in who builds it more than in what it does. She leans on family, faith and routine as her anchors. The family's three generations at this mine give her a strong sense of belonging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the companies should look after the people who built them. The new owners have already cut our pay scale, so I'd expect them to cut jobs too. I'd say that at work, and I'd say it to anyone who says it's progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it scares me, because Mark and I are both at the same mine. If they automate the loaders and the trucks need fewer mechanics, we could both be cut in the same round. That's the thing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any spending that's not needed, no holidays, no new phones, and get the car paid off faster. I'd ask the foreman straight out what's planned for the ROM pad. And I'd talk to Mark about whether one of us should look for work outside the mine, so we're not both in the same basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, in my stomach. Like hearing a rumour about layoffs on a Friday and having to wait the whole weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider training for one of the new jobs, like remote operation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I've seen the remote room at the iron ore mine on a video, people sitting at screens all day. That's not mining to me. I'd rather find another job with my hands, even if it pays less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if things got hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the church. Mark's mum, my brother who runs the hardware shop in town, and our pastor knows everyone who's hiring. I'd take any job before I'd take a handout.

S1.say: She'd say companies should look after the people who built them, and expects the new owners, who already cut pay scales, to cut jobs too. She'd challenge anyone calling it progress.
S1.think: It scares her because she and her husband work at the same mine and could both be cut in one round. That's what keeps her awake.
S1.do: Cuts all non-essential spending and pays off the car faster. Asks the foreman directly about plans for the ROM pad and talks with her husband about one of them finding work outside the mine.
S1.feel: Worried in her stomach, like waiting all weekend after a layoff rumour.
S1.quote: I'd take any job before I'd take a handout.
S1.fieldNote: The main risk she sees is both household incomes tied to one employer. She rejects remote control room work as not real mining and would rather do lower-paid hands-on work. Her support network is family, her brother's shop and the church, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let big tech companies run the world. Nobody asked us. I'd say it to anyone, and I'd vote for whoever promised to stand up for working towns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd lose everything. Both of us at the same mine, no savings to speak of, and every job in town going to machines at once. I don't see how we keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years I'd pay off the car and save every cent, and Mark would pick up repair jobs on the side. When it hit, we'd go to the bank before we missed a payment. If it came to it, we'd move in with Mark's mum, she's got the room, and we'd lean on the church. I'd take cleaning work, anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I'd pray a lot, and I'd still be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years of warning, is there anything you'd do differently in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'm not going to become something else in two years. I'd just hold on tighter and try to keep the kids from seeing how scared we were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah and Luke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That God has a plan and the family sticks together. Luke would be fine at Nana's, he loves it there. Hannah would be angry, she's 14, everything's the end of the world already.

S2.say: She'd blame big tech companies for running the world without asking working people. She'd vote for whoever promised to stand up for working towns.
S2.think: She expects to lose everything, with both incomes at one mine, no savings and every local job going at once. She can't see how they keep the house.
S2.do: Pays off the car and saves every cent in the two years before while her husband takes side repair jobs. Goes to the bank before missing payments, moves in with her mother-in-law if needed, leans on the church and takes cleaning work or anything else.
S2.feel: Panicked; praying a lot and still lying awake.
S2.quote: I'd just hold on tighter and try to keep the kids from seeing how scared we were.
S2.fieldNote: She sees no way to change course in two years and doesn't try to. Her faith and family are what she reaches for, along with any work at all. Her anger is aimed at big tech, and she'd act on it at the ballot box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to make the politicians listen. I'd want rules that a mine can't replace locals with robots without paying the town back. And I'd say families need to pull together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years doesn't save my job, it just puts it off. I'd be 48. But it might give Mark time to find something steadier, maybe at my brother's hardware shop, so we're not both at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and pay down the car and then the mortgage. I'd push Mark to move to the hardware shop in the first year or two, even for less money, so one of us is off the mine. I'd vote for whoever is talking about local jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I'd have something to do. Like knowing a big storm is coming in a few days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a hardware shop survive this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd hope people still want someone to tell them which screw to use. But robots could stack shelves. I'm hoping it buys us a few years, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you won't retrain. Would five years change your mind at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was a proper apprenticeship, with hands-on work and an older tradesperson teaching me, maybe. Not sitting at a screen. My dad did his fitter's apprenticeship at 30 and he always said it was the best thing he did.

S3.say: She'd say there are five years to make politicians listen, with rules that mines can't replace locals with robots without paying the town back. She'd say families need to pull together.
S3.think: Five years only delays losing her job, and she'd be 48. It might give her husband time to move somewhere steadier, like her brother's hardware shop.
S3.do: Keeps working and pays down the car and then the mortgage. Pushes her husband to move to her brother's hardware shop in the first year or two, even for less pay, and votes for whoever talks about local jobs.
S3.feel: Alarmed, but with something to do, like a storm coming in a few days.
S3.quote: My dad did his fitter's apprenticeship at 30 and he always said it was the best thing he did.
S3.fieldNote: Her strategy is to split the household's risk by getting one partner off the mine. She'd consider an old-style apprenticeship, drawing on her father's example, but not screen work. Her politics are about protecting local jobs, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the country to make sure working people aren't thrown away. I'd want apprenticeships brought back properly, in the towns, not just in cities. And I'd say it at church and in the school car park.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is better, but I still don't know what I'd do. I'd be 53, and I can't picture myself anywhere but the ROM pad. I'd probably just ride it out as long as they'd keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to pay off as much of the mortgage as I could, putting every spare dollar on it. I'd get Mark off the mine within a few years. And I'd push Hannah and Luke toward trades with apprenticeships, maybe electrical for Hannah, she's good with her hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, a lot, but not like the fast one. I'd have time to pray on it and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why still so worried, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years doesn't change who I am. I'm a loader driver at a nickel mine and I'm not going to be anything else. The time helps the kids more than it helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad have said about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say the mine's had bad years before, keep your head down and your boots clean. But he never saw anything like this. I think he'd be frightened too, and he'd never say so.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough for the country to protect working people and bring back proper apprenticeships in towns. She'd say it at church and in the school car park.
S4.think: Ten years is better, but she still can't picture herself anywhere but the stockpile. At 53 she'd probably ride it out as long as they keep her.
S4.do: Puts every spare dollar on the mortgage and gets her husband off the mine within a few years. Pushes her children toward trades with apprenticeships, such as electrical work for her daughter.
S4.feel: Still very worried, but with time to pray and plan.
S4.quote: Ten years doesn't change who I am. I'm a loader driver at a nickel mine and I'm not going to be anything else.
S4.fieldNote: More time helps her children's chances but not her own sense of who she is. She stays alarmed because her identity and her job are tied together. She leans on her father's memory to make sense of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Mark and I both lose our jobs, there's nothing else in town, and we've got almost nothing saved. What would help is real jobs, not handouts, and rules that say if a company replaces a whole town with robots, it has to put something back, like apprenticeships and work for the people who built it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. When things get hard here, it's the church that runs the food drive and finds people work. Nobody from the city ever asks about that, and it matters more than any app.

headlineQuote: When things get hard here, it's the church that runs the food drive and finds people work.
portrait: Chloe Novak is a 43-year-old front-end loader operator on the stockpile at a nickel mine where her grandfather and father also worked. She and her husband, a diesel mechanic, both work at the mine on lower pay scales, with two children, a mortgage and almost no savings. She distrusts AI and the people who build it, won't retrain for screen work, and would take any hands-on job before a handout. Her plans across the scenarios centre on splitting the family's risk, leaning on family and church, and steering her children toward apprenticeships.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she and her husband would both lose their jobs with nothing else in town and almost nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Real jobs rather than handouts, and rules making companies that replace a town's workers with robots put something back, like apprenticeships and work.
